title: Cache without lying
summary: Add a cache-aside read and a write path that invalidates instead of serving stale rows.

scenario.briefing: Product pages read from PostgreSQL on every request. The team added Redis, but the first version served a price that was five minutes old and fell over when Redis restarted.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Review an artifact and identify the concrete risks.

hints: Cache-aside: read Redis, fall back to PostgreSQL, then fill Redis with a TTL.
Update the database first, then delete the cached key.
Coalesce concurrent misses so one refresh does not stampede the database.
Treat Redis errors as a cache miss, not a request failure.

misconceptions.description: Treating the cache as the source of truth.
misconceptions.testDescription: Reads use the cache with an explicit TTL.
misconceptions.feedback: A cache is a copy. The database remains authoritative, and the request must still work when the cache is down.

misconceptions.description: Updating the database after overwriting the cache.
misconceptions.feedback: Writing the cache first lets a failed database write leave a fresh-looking stale value. Update the database, then invalidate the cache.

misconceptions.description: Relying on a TTL to fix write-order bugs.
misconceptions.testDescription: The write path updates the database before deleting the cached key.
misconceptions.feedback: A TTL only bounds staleness. It does not repair an incorrect write order.

sections.title: The database is the source of truth
sections.body: A cache holds a copy. Read Redis first, fall back to PostgreSQL on a miss, and fill Redis with a TTL. The TTL bounds how long a bad copy can survive; it does not make the copy correct.

sections.title: Invalidate after the write commits
sections.body: Update the database, then delete the key. Never write a value that was read before the update, because that turns a stale read into a stale cache entry. A reader that loaded before the commit can still refill the key with the old value; the TTL bounds that window, and a versioned key closes it when freshness must be strict.

sections.title: Stampedes and outages
sections.body: A hot key that expires can send many requests to the database at once. Coalesce misses in the process, and use a shared lock when several processes share the cache. If Redis is down, serve from the database instead of failing the request.

vocabulary.definition: The application reads the cache, loads from the database on a miss, and fills the cache.
The time a cached entry is allowed to live before it expires.
Removing or replacing a cached entry when the source data changes.
Many requests hitting the database at once when a popular key expires.
The system that owns the data and decides what is correct.

steps.title: Cache product reads safely
steps.prompt: Edit cache.ts. Read through the cache with a 300-second TTL, coalesce concurrent misses, fall back to the database when Redis fails, and delete the cached key after a successful update.

tests.description: Reads use the cache with an explicit TTL.
A miss loads from the database and fills the cache.
Concurrent misses are coalesced in this process.
includes: const inFlight = new Map<string, Promise<Product | null>>();

tests.description: The write path updates the database before deleting the cached key.
Cache failures fall back to the database instead of failing the request.

hints: Name the source of truth before adding a cache.
Set a TTL on every cached value.
Coalesce concurrent misses and fall back when Redis fails.
Update the database first, then delete the cached key, and never serve cache data as authoritative.

steps.title: Review the price update
steps.prompt: Review the artifact and select every real caching problem.

artifact.title: updatePrice.ts
artifact.caption: The function runs after an admin changes a price.

findings.label: The product is read before the update, so the cache is filled with the old price.
The write path overwrites the key instead of deleting it, so the stale value survives for the TTL.
The TTL limits the staleness window but does not make the cached value correct.
A row lock on the update would prevent the stale cache value.
Writing the cache makes it the source of truth, so the stale price is acceptable.

verdicts.label: Block the change until the cache is invalidated from the updated row.
Ship it; the TTL makes the old price acceptable.

steps.explanation: The cache write happens after the update but stores the row read before it. Delete the key after the update commits, or cache the row returned by the update. A TTL only bounds the damage.
hints: Find where the cache can outlive the database value.
Check the write order and the TTL.
Ask what happens when Redis is unavailable.
Block the change: stale reads and cache-as-truth are correctness bugs.
